title: The past: irregular preterite
objectives: I can tell a regular preterite from an irregular one by looking at where the stress falls and how the form ends.
I can use the preterite of ser, ir, ter, estar, fazer, dar, ver, vir, poder, querer, dizer, trazer, pôr and saber.
I can recognize and produce the irregular stems (tiv-, estiv-, fiz-, quis-, diss-, troux-, pus-, soub-) and explain how each form is spelled and pronounced.
I can narrate a short story or a trip in sequence with primeiro, depois, em seguida, então and por fim.
I can ask and answer questions such as Você já foi ao Rio? with the simple past, and explain why Portuguese does not use tenho plus a participle for a single experience.

vocabulary.note: Spelled with the diphthong ei, pri-MEI-ro. Also an ordinal number (o primeiro dia, the first day), and then it agrees with its noun: a primeira vez.

example.target: Primeiro eu tomei café e depois saí de casa.
example.source: First I had coffee and then I left home.
example.source_literal: First I took coffee and afterwards I-left of house.

vocabulary.note: Stressed on the last syllable, de-POIS, as its ending predicts. The initial e is weak and often said i, so the d before it says j as in jeans. Before a noun it needs de: depois de, which fuses with an article (do, da).

example.target: Depois do jantar, nós fomos passear.
example.source: After dinner, we went for a walk.
example.source_literal: Afterwards of-the dinner, we went to-stroll.

vocabulary.note: Seguida comes from seguir, to follow, so the phrase means right after what was just said. In gui the u is silent and only keeps the g hard: se-GUI-da, with a weak final a.

example.target: Em seguida, ela abriu o presente.
example.source: Next, she opened the present.
example.source_literal: In following, she opened the present.

vocabulary.note: Ão is a nasal diphthong and already marks the stress on the last syllable (en-TÃO), so it needs no second accent. In stories it means 'then' for the next event, and 'so' when what follows is a result.

example.target: Perdi o ônibus, então fui a pé.
example.source: I missed the bus, so I walked.
example.source_literal: I-lost the bus, then I-went on foot.

vocabulary.note: Fim has a nasal vowel: the m only nasalizes the i, so the lips do not close. Por here is the small unstressed preposition, with no circumflex; the circumflex belongs to the stressed verb pôr.

example.target: Por fim, eles chegaram ao hotel.
example.source: Finally, they reached the hotel.
example.source_literal: For end, they arrived at-the hotel.

vocabulary.note: No is em plus o fused into one word. In seguinte the n only nasalizes the vowel, gui keeps a silent u, and the t before the weak final e says ch: se-GUIN-chi.

example.target: No dia seguinte, a gente acordou tarde.
example.source: The next day, we woke up late.
example.source_literal: On-the day following, the people woke-up late.

vocabulary.note: Ai is a diphthong, one syllable. In tarde the d stands before a weak final e, which is said i, so the d says j as in jeans: TAR-ji.

example.target: Mais tarde, ele me disse a verdade.
example.source: Later, he told me the truth.
example.source_literal: More late, he me said the truth.

vocabulary.note: Ends in -gem: g before e says zh as in measure, and em is a nasal ending. The default for em puts the stress on the second to last syllable, vi-A-gem. Plural: viagens.

example.target: A viagem pra Salvador foi ótima.
example.source: The trip to Salvador was great.

vocabulary.note: Always plural in Portuguese. Fé-ri-as has three beats because the ia at the end counts as two, so the stress is third from the end and an accent is always written, as in história.

example.target: Passamos as férias em Florianópolis.
example.source: We spent our vacation in Florianópolis.

vocabulary.note: Regular in the preterite: nasci, nasceu. The sc says plain s: nas-CER. English forms 'was born' with a helper verb; Portuguese uses the plain preterite, eu nasci.

example.target: Eu nasci em Recife, mas cresci em Brasília.
example.source: I was born in Recife, but I grew up in Brasília.

vocabulary.note: Reflexive, with se before the verb: eu me formei, ela se formou. Formar means to form or shape, so the idea is to shape yourself into a professional.

example.target: Minha prima se formou em medicina.
example.source: My cousin graduated in medicine.
example.source_literal: My cousin herself formed in medicine.

vocabulary.source: to meet, to get to know
vocabulary.note: Nh says ny as in canyon, and c before e says s: co-nhe-CER. Conhecer means to be acquainted with a person or place, so in the preterite it means to meet for the first time or to get to know. Se conhecer, with se, means to meet each other.

example.target: Conheci minha esposa numa festa.
example.source: I met my wife at a party.

vocabulary.note: Ficar also means to become or to get, when a state follows: fiquei com vergonha is I got embarrassed, and o mar ficou agitado is the sea became rough. The literal idea is remaining in a state. The eu form is fiquei: c becomes qu before the ending -ei so that the sound stays k, the same change as tocar to toquei. A spelling change that only protects a sound does not make a verb irregular.

example.target: Ficamos num hotel perto da praia.
example.source: We stayed in a hotel near the beach.
example.source_literal: We-stayed in-a hotel near of-the beach.

vocabulary.note: Preterite: fui, foi, fomos, foram, identical to the preterite of ser. Fui is a diphthong, one syllable.

example.target: Fui ao mercado de manhã.
example.source: I went to the market in the morning.

vocabulary.note: Preterite: vi, viu, vimos, viram. Ver also means to watch (ver um filme).

example.target: Vimos o Cristo Redentor de perto.
example.source: We saw Christ the Redeemer up close.
example.source_literal: We-saw the Christ Redeemer of near.

vocabulary.note: Preterite: vim, veio, viemos, vieram. Present: venho, vem, vimos, vêm. Vir is movement toward the place where the speaker is or will be; ir is movement away from it.

example.target: Meus primos vieram me visitar no Natal.
example.source: My cousins came to visit me at Christmas.
example.source_literal: My cousins came me to-visit in-the Christmas.

vocabulary.note: Preterite: trouxe, trouxe, trouxemos, trouxeram. The stem is troux-: ou is a diphthong, often said as a plain closed o, and x after the diphthong ou says sh, as it does after ai and ei in caixa and peixe, so trouxe is TROH-shee.

example.target: Ela trouxe um presente do Rio.
example.source: She brought a present from Rio.
example.source_literal: She brought a present of-the Rio.

vocabulary.note: Preterite: disse, disse, dissemos, disseram. The stem is diss-, and ss between vowels says s. In speech, falar is often used instead. In me disse the small word me means to me and goes before the verb; object pronouns get their own unit later.

example.target: Ele disse que gostou da viagem.
example.source: He said he liked the trip.
example.source_literal: He said that he-liked of-the trip.

vocabulary.note: Preterite: pus, pôs, pusemos, puseram. The circumflex keeps the stressed verb pôr apart from the small unstressed preposition por. Pôr a mesa is to set the table; o pôr do sol is the sunset.

example.target: Pus as malas no carro.
example.source: I put the suitcases in the car.

vocabulary.note: Preterite: tive, teve, tivemos, tiveram. Ter sorte, literally to have luck, is the way to say to be lucky. In tive the t says ch because it stands before the sound i; in teve it stays t.

example.target: Tivemos sorte com o tempo.
example.source: We were lucky with the weather.

vocabulary.note: Also to make. Preterite: fiz, fez, fizemos, fizeram. Fiz and fez are one syllable ending in z, so they carry no accent.

example.target: O que você fez ontem à noite?
example.source: What did you do last night?
example.source_literal: What you did yesterday at-the night?

vocabulary.note: Preterite: pude, pôde, pudemos, puderam. In the preterite it states what happened on one occasion: não pude means I could not and so I did not.

example.target: Ontem eu não pude ir à aula.
example.source: Yesterday I could not go to class.
example.source_literal: Yesterday I not could go to-the class.

grammar.title: Regular or irregular: stem, ending and stress
grammar.explanation:
The preterite (pretérito perfeito) is the tense for an action that is finished: it happened, it is over, and the speaker presents it as one completed event. A tense is the form of the verb that places the action in time. The previous unit built regular preterites from two parts: the stem (the infinitive without -ar, -er or -ir) and an ending that shows who acted. The stem fal- plus the endings -ei, -ou, -amos, -aram gives falei, falou, falamos, falaram. A verb is irregular when its forms do not follow that recipe, so each form has to be learned.

The commonest verbs are the irregular ones, and there is a reason. A word used constantly is never rebuilt from rules; speakers keep its old, worn forms, while a rare word is rebuilt by the recipe every time. English shows the same split: be, go, have, do, say and see break the -ed rule (was, went, had, did, said, saw), and rare verbs follow it. The irregular Portuguese preterites are survivors of the Latin past tense, in which the stem itself changed, as English changes the vowel in sing and sang, instead of an ending being added.

There is a dependable way to see the pattern, and it is stress. Stress is the syllable that is said louder and longer, as the lesson on stress explained. In the eu and você forms of a regular preterite the stress sits on the ending: fa-LEI, fa-LOU, co-MEU, par-TIU. In the eu and você forms of the irregular stem verbs of this unit the stress sits on the stem: TI-ve, TE-ve, FEZ, PU-de, DIS-se. Traditional grammars call these the strong preterites, because the stem carries the weight. For the você form the test is quick: if it ends in -ou, -eu or -iu it is regular (falou, comeu, partiu); if it ends in a plain -e or in a consonant (teve, fez, disse, pôs) the stem is irregular and stressed. Vir, with veio, is the one odd shape. One caution: deu and viu also end in -eu and -iu, so the test cannot prove a verb regular by itself. Dar and ver are irregular in the way they borrow endings from another family, which the fourth note explains.

The irregular verbs of this unit fall into three groups. Ser and ir share one set of forms. The stem verbs (ter, estar, fazer, poder, querer, dizer, trazer, saber, pôr and vir) have a new stem and special eu and você forms. Dar and ver keep a short shape but borrow the endings of another verb family. Everything else is regular: nascer, conhecer, ficar, chegar, sair and the rest. A spelling change such as ficar becoming fiquei is not irregularity, because it only protects a sound, as the previous unit showed.

grammar.title: Ser and ir share one preterite
grammar.explanation:
Ser (to be) and ir (to go) are different verbs with different meanings, but in the preterite they have exactly one set of forms: fui, foi, fomos, foram. Historically ir lost its own preterite and the forms of ser took over. English has the same oddity in a small way (the verb go borrows went from another verb), but Portuguese goes further: the two verbs are spelled and said identically, so you never choose a form, you only decide which verb you are reading or writing.

The context decides, and the test is the destination. If a place follows and the idea is movement toward it, the verb is ir: Fui ao mercado, I went to the market. If the sentence describes someone or something (an adjective, a profession, a noun) or says where or when an event took place, the verb is ser: A festa foi ótima. The small word before the place helps. After ir the place comes with a or para (to), and after ser it comes with em (at, in): A festa foi na casa da Ana, mas eu fui só às dez. Both verbs are in that sentence, 'The party was at Ana's house, but I only went at ten'.

How ir joins its destination. The preposition a (to) fuses with the article into one word: a plus o gives ao, a plus a gives à, a plus os gives aos, a plus as gives às. The grave accent on à only records the fusion, as the accents lesson explained. Para stays separate from the article, and in speech para becomes pra and para o becomes pro: Fui pra praia. Many Brazilians also use em for a destination, as in Fui no mercado and Fui na casa dela; it is extremely common in speech, and careful writing prefers a or para. City names with no article take the preposition directly: Fui a Salvador, Fui pra Salvador.

Pronunciation follows the rules of the first lessons. Fui is the diphthong ui, said as one quick beat, FWEE; foi is the diphthong oi, like English 'foy'. Fomos and foram have the stress on the first syllable because the endings os and am predict it, so no accent is written.

The preterite presents a finished whole, so foi as a form of ser fits events and completed spans of time: A prova foi difícil, Eles foram professores por dez anos. Descriptions of how things used to be belong to another past tense, taught later. As in the present, a gente takes the foi form: A gente foi ao cinema. Como foi a viagem? is the standard question about how a finished trip went; it uses ser, and the answer is a judgment of the whole event.

examples.target: Ontem eu fui ao dentista.
examples.source: Yesterday I went to the dentist.

examples.target: A prova foi muito difícil.
examples.source: The test was very difficult.

examples.target: Nós fomos pra praia no feriado.
examples.source: We went to the beach on the holiday.

examples.target: Eles foram professores nessa escola por dez anos.
examples.source: They were teachers at that school for ten years.
examples.source_literal: They were teachers in-that school for ten years.

examples.target: Como foi a sua viagem?
examples.source: How was your trip?
examples.source_literal: How was the your trip?

examples.target: A festa foi na casa da Ana, mas eu fui só às dez.
examples.source: The party was at Ana's house, but I only went at ten.
examples.source_literal: The party was in-the house of-the Ana, but I went only at-the ten.

grammar.title: The stem verbs: ter, estar, fazer, poder, querer, dizer, trazer, saber, pôr, vir
grammar.explanation:
Ten verbs build their preterite on a new stem instead of the stem of the infinitive, and the stress sits on that stem, which is what the previous note gave as the mark of a strong preterite. The stems are tiv- (ter), estiv- (estar), fiz- or fez- (fazer), pud- or pôd- (poder), quis- (querer), diss- (dizer), troux- (trazer), soub- (saber), pus- or pôs- (pôr), and for vir the forms vim and veio. The endings fall into two halves.

The nós and eles forms are ordinary. Add -emos and -eram to the new stem: tivemos, tiveram; fizemos, fizeram. These are the same endings as comer (comemos, comeram). The eu and você forms are the special ones, because they lack the regular -ei and -ou. The eu form ends in a short -e (tive, estive, pude, disse, trouxe, soube) or has no vowel ending at all (fiz, quis, pus, vim). The você form is the same stem with -e or nothing: teve, esteve, pôde, disse, trouxe, soube, fez, quis, pôs. Only veio is a different shape.

The second pattern is the vowel. In five verbs the eu form has a high vowel, i or u, where the você form has e or ô: tive and teve, estive and esteve, fiz and fez, pude and pôde, pus and pôs. This comes from an ancient sound change. The old first person ended in -i, and that i pulled the vowel of the stem up. You do not need the Latin, only the effect: i or u in the eu form, e or ô in the você form. Where the stem vowel is i or ou and does not alternate (disse, quis, trouxe, soube), the eu and você forms are identical: Eu disse and Ele disse. The subject pronoun, or the context, then shows who spoke.

Use follows from the tense. The preterite presents an action as a complete event, so Tive uma ideia means 'I had an idea' at a given moment, and Não pude ir means 'I could not go' on that occasion: it did not happen. Querer and saber shift their meaning in the preterite (quis, 'I wanted' at that moment; soube, 'I found out'); a later unit returns to this. Compare the present tense of the same verbs, which you know, and notice that the preterite stem is often quite different from the present stem (faz, but fiz; tem, but tive).

examples.target: Eu tive uma ideia muito boa.
examples.source: I had a very good idea.

examples.target: A gente esteve em Paris no ano passado.
examples.source: We were in Paris last year.
examples.source_literal: The people was in Paris in-the year past.

examples.source: She made a chocolate cake for the party.

examples.target: Eles trouxeram vinho e pão.
examples.source: They brought wine and bread.

examples.source: I could not go to the wedding.
examples.source_literal: I not could go to-the wedding.

examples.target: O gerente disse que a reunião acabou.
examples.source: The manager said that the meeting ended.

grammar.title: Dar and ver, and the trap between viram and vieram
grammar.explanation:
Dar (to give) and ver (to see) are irregular in a different way from the stem verbs. There is no new stem with a moving stress. These are short verbs whose preterite endings come from another family, and the forms end up very short. Vir (to come), which was in the previous table, is included here because its forms are easily confused with those of ver.

Dar is an -ar verb, but most of its preterite uses the -er family: dei, deu, demos, deram (compare comi, comeu, comemos, comeram; dei keeps the -ei of the -ar family). Ver is an -er verb whose preterite uses the -ir family: vi, viu, vimos, viram (compare parti, partiu, partimos, partiram). Vir has the most changed forms: vim, veio, viemos, vieram, with the ordinary endings -emos and -eram in the plural. None of these forms carries an accent mark, because in each the stress falls where the default for its ending predicts: DEU, VI, vi-E-mos, VEI-o, DE-ram.

First trap: viram (they saw) and vieram (they came), and vimos (we saw) and viemos (we came). They differ by one letter and one beat. Viram has two syllables, VI-ram, stressed on the first. Vieram has three, vi-E-ram, stressed on the e, which is the second to last syllable as the ending am predicts. Listen for that extra e. Vimos is also the present of vir (we come), so the time words around it tell you which tense you are reading.

Second trap: ir and vir both mean motion, and the difference is direction relative to the speaker. Ir moves away from where the speaker is now, or toward a place the speaker is not. Vir moves toward where the speaker is or will be: Meus amigos vieram à minha casa, 'My friends came to my house'. English go and come divide the work in nearly the same way, but Portuguese is stricter. When someone calls you and you answer 'I'm coming!', Portuguese says Já vou!, with ir, because you are moving away from where you are now.

The sequencing words of the next note combine with these forms in stories: Primeiro a gente viu o jogo, depois dançou, por fim voltou pra casa.

examples.target: Eu dei um livro de presente pra minha mãe.
examples.source: I gave my mother a book as a present.
examples.source_literal: I gave a book of gift for my mother.

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: reading and writing the irregular forms
grammar.explanation:
Every written form in this unit can be read and written with rules you already have, and three of them do almost all the work. First, an accent mark appears where a word breaks the default stress of its ending, where it tells two words apart, or where it keeps a stressed i or u from joining the vowel before it (a hiatus). Second, letters choose their sound from the letters beside them: a single s between vowels says z, ss says s, qu keeps the k sound before i, and x after the diphthongs ai, ei and ou says sh. Third, in most of Brazil t and d say ch and j before the sound i, and a final unstressed e is said i. Reading an irregular preterite is therefore no new skill; it is the reading procedure of the first lessons applied to new words.

The eu form against the você form. Tive and teve differ in one letter, and the rules explain how they sound. The eu form has the vowel i, so the t before it says ch as in cheese: tive is CHEE-vee. The você form has a stressed e, which is not the sound i, so the t stays a plain t: teve is TAY-vee, where AY stands for the closed e, the vowel of 'say' held steady without its glide. Estive is is-CHEE-vee and esteve is is-TAY-vee in the same way. The rule works for d too. Pude ends in an unstressed e, said i, so its d says j as in jeans: POO-jee. Pôde is POH-jee, with a closed o. But in pudemos and puderam the d stands before a stressed e and stays plain: poo-DAY-moos. Disse begins with d before the vowel i, so it says JEE-see, and dissemos is jee-SAY-moos.

The letters s, ss and z. A single s between two vowels says z, and the doubled ss exists to write the sound s in that position. So the spelling tells you the sound: pusemos is poo-ZAY-moos and quisemos is kee-ZAY-moos, while dissemos, with ss, says s. Fizemos is spelled with a z and says z. The final z of fiz and fez follows the regional choice for a syllable-final s: s in São Paulo and sh in Rio. In quis and quisemos the u of qu is silent and only keeps the k sound before i: KEES.

The letter x and the diphthong ou. In trouxe the x says sh, as it does after the diphthongs ai and ei in caixa and peixe. Not every x after a diphthong follows this: in auxílio it says s, so the pattern is learned for ai, ei and ou. The ou of trouxe and soube is often said as a plain closed o in everyday speech: TROH-shee and SOH-bee.

Vowel pairs. Fui and foi are diphthongs of one beat each: fui is one quick FWEE, foi is like English 'foy'. Veio is vei-o, two syllables stressed on vei: the e and i form the diphthong ei and the final o is said u, so VAY-oo. Vieram is different: it is written vi-e-ram, three beats, and the stress falls on the e, so vee-AY-ram, whereas viram is VEE-ram, two beats. Neither needs an accent, because the stress is where the default for its ending (am or o) predicts.

Accents in this unit. Pôde is stressed where the default puts it, so its circumflex has one job: it shows a closed o and separates pôde (he could, once) from pode (he can), which has an open o. Pôr is the stressed infinitive, and its circumflex separates it from the small unstressed por (by, through). Pôs is a one-syllable word ending in os, and a stressed one-syllable word ending in a, e or o (with or without s) always takes a mark; the vowel is closed, so the mark is the circumflex. Pus and quis end in us and is, and fiz and fez end in z, so none of them needs a mark. Eles tiveram and eles vieram have no accent, because the ending am puts the stress on the second to last syllable (ti-VE-ram, vi-E-ram). The present plural têm and vêm keep a circumflex only to show that they are plural in writing, since in Brazilian speech tem and têm sound the same.

Other words in the unit's texts. Words stressed on the third to last syllable always take a mark, and the vowel chooses it: ótima, sábado, rápido, último. Férias follows the same logic because the ia at the end counts as two beats. Acarajé is stressed on the last syllable, which breaks the default for a final e, so it takes an acute, and the e is open. Saí has a stressed i alone in its syllable next to another vowel, which is a hiatus, so the accent is written. Ideia has no accent since the 2009 spelling agreement, because the open ei of a word stressed on the second to last syllable lost its mark.

grammar.title: Sequencing a story, and why Brazilians use the simple past
grammar.explanation:
A story is a chain of finished events, and Portuguese puts each event of the chain in the preterite, in the order in which things happened. The order of the sentences carries the time, and connectors make it explicit: primeiro (first), depois (afterwards), em seguida (next), então (then, or so when a result follows), mais tarde (later), no dia seguinte (the next day) and por fim (finally). Adding a connector never changes the verb: Primeiro eu fui ao banco, depois fiz compras e por fim voltei pra casa. Two of the connectors are built from ordinary words that show what they do: em seguida is 'in following' and por fim is 'for end'.

English divides the past in a way Portuguese does not. English has a present perfect, made with 'have' and a participle. A participle is the form of a verb used after 'have', such as 'studied' or 'been' in 'I have studied' and 'I have been'. English needs the present perfect to speak of an experience whose time you do not mention: 'Have you ever been to Rio?' The plain past, 'Did you go to Rio?', seems to demand a particular time. Portuguese has no such restriction. Its preterite works with or without a stated time, so a single past experience is the preterite plus the adverb já or nunca. Já means 'already', and in a question it means 'ever'; nunca means 'never'. Você já foi ao Rio? Nunca fui. Já comi acarajé.

Portuguese does have a compound tense built from tenho (the present of ter) and a participle in -ado or -ido: tenho estudado. It does not match the English present perfect. It describes an action that has been repeating or continuing up to now: Tenho estudado muito ultimamente means 'I have been studying a lot lately'. The ending -mente turns an adjective into an adverb, as -ly does in English, and ultimamente means 'lately', not 'ultimately'. So 'Have you ever been to Salvador?' is Você já foi a Salvador?, never Você tem ido a Salvador?. In everyday Brazilian speech the simple past does almost all of this work and the compound form is rare.

culture.title: Feriados, feriadões and holiday trips
culture.text:
Brazilians love a long weekend. A feriadão, literally a big holiday because the ending -ão makes a word bigger, is a holiday that falls on a Monday or Friday, or that can be joined to the weekend by taking a single day off, which people call emendar o feriado, literally to splice the holiday. When a holiday lands on a Tuesday or Thursday, many offices treat the day between it and the weekend as a ponte, a bridge, and people travel for four or five days. Highways to the coast fill up, and bus stations and airports are crowded, so many people leave very early or on the night before.

The most famous holiday is Carnaval, held in February or March, with street parties called blocos in Rio, São Paulo, Salvador, Recife and Olinda. In Salvador you can follow a trio elétrico, a truck with a band on top, and in Recife and Olinda the frevo orchestras. Other important moments are the Festas Juninas in June, with quadrilha dancing and food made from corn, Natal at the end of the year, and Réveillon on December 31, when many Brazilians wear white and, in coastal cities, watch fireworks on the beach.

When friends return from a trip, the first thing people ask is Como foi a viagem? Travelers are expected to bring a lembrancinha, a small souvenir, literally a little memory. A classic example is the colorful fitinha do Senhor do Bonfim from Salvador, a little ribbon which you tie around your wrist with three knots and a wish.

exercises.prompt: Match each preterite form with its infinitive
In which sentence is foi a form of ser, not of ir?
exercises.explanation: Ser and ir share one preterite, so the context decides. Muito simpático describes the person and no destination follows, so this is ser. The other three name a place reached with a or pra, which means movement.

exercises.hint_source: Yesterday I went to the supermarket.
exercises.explanation: A destination introduced by a (ao is a plus o) shows movement, so the verb is ir. Fui is the eu form of both ir and ser.
Muito longo describes the film and no destination follows, so the verb is ser. Ser and ir share the form foi.

choices: Yesterday we went to the cinema.

exercises.prompt: Which pair gives the eu form and the você form of fazer in the preterite?
exercises.explanation: The eu form has the high vowel i (fiz) and the você form has e (fez). The same alternation appears in tive and teve, and pude and pôde.

exercises.prompt: A regular você form ends in -ou, -eu or -iu, with the stress on that ending. Which of these você forms is therefore irregular?
exercises.explanation: Disse ends in a plain -e and is stressed on the stem, DIS-se, which marks a strong preterite. Falou, comeu and partiu are stressed on their endings.

exercises.prompt: Why is pôde written with a circumflex?
choices: It shows that the stress is on the last syllable.
It separates the preterite pôde from the present pode, which has an open o.
Every irregular preterite carries a circumflex.
exercises.explanation: Pôde is stressed where the default puts it, so the mark is not needed for stress. It is a differential accent: closed o in pôde, he could, against open o in pode, he can.

exercises.hint_source: I saw Marina at the party.
exercises.explanation: Ver is an -er verb whose preterite takes -ir endings on the stem v-: vi, viu, vimos, viram.

exercises.prompt: Deu ends in -eu, like the regular comeu. Which statement is correct?
choices: Deu is regular, because every form ending in -eu is regular.
Deu is from dar, an -ar verb that borrows -er endings, so the ending alone cannot prove a verb regular.
Deu is from ser, which shares its preterite with ir.
Deu is a stem verb with the stem deu-.
exercises.explanation: Dar is an -ar verb, but its preterite dei, deu, demos, deram uses the -er endings. The -eu test only works together with the infinitive: an -ar verb should give -ou.

exercises.prompt_target: Ele ___ ir, mas eu não pude.
exercises.hint_source: He was able to go, but I could not.
exercises.explanation: The eu form has the high vowel u (pude) and the você form has the closed ô (pôde). The circumflex also separates it from the present pode, which has an open o.

exercises.prompt: Why does the i of saí and aí carry an accent?
choices: It is a stressed vowel standing alone next to another vowel (a hiatus), so the stress is written.
It separates two words that would otherwise look the same.
Every word that ends in i takes an accent.
exercises.explanation: In sa-Í and a-Í the a and the i belong to different syllables, so no diphthong forms, and the stressed i is marked. Words such as fui, where the two vowels form one beat, need no accent.

exercises.prompt: Which syllable of vieram carries the stress?
exercises.explanation: The ending am puts the stress on the second to last syllable, so vi-E-ram. Viram, they saw, has two syllables and is stressed on the first.

exercises.prompt: You are at home and your cousins arrive at your house. Which verb describes their movement toward you?
exercises.explanation: Vir is movement toward the place where the speaker is. Ir is movement away from it.

exercises.explanation: A single s between two vowels says z, and ss exists to write the sound s there. That is why dissemos, spelled with ss, says s.

exercises.explanation: After the diphthong ou, x says sh, as it does after ai and ei in caixa and peixe. The e at the end is weak and said i: TROH-shee.
